- **self**: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS (30/7)

## Definitions

- [statement] The INVEST publication is a protocol for a planned open-label randomized comparison of DBS and continuous intrajejunal levodopa, with ancillary preference cohorts and quality-of-life and economic outcomes. Its planned sample and methods must not be cited as completed efficacy or cost-effectiveness results. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6995127/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS

## How it works

- [statement] Device-aided therapy is considered when oral or transdermal treatment inadequately controls disabling motor fluctuations or dyskinesia; options include apomorphine infusion, intestinal levodopa infusion, subcutaneous levodopa infusion and DBS. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592668/
- [statement] Important burdens differ by modality: apomorphine can cause skin nodules, nausea and hypotension; intestinal levodopa can cause tube obstruction or displacement and abdominal complications; subcutaneous foslevodopa can cause infusion-site reactions or infections; DBS carries surgical and hardware risks. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592668/
- [statement] Device-aided therapy is considered when optimized oral treatment no longer adequately controls Parkinson motor complications; the established options include DBS, continuous subcutaneous apomorphine and intestinal levodopa infusion, with subcutaneous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa adding another delivery option. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3825542/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Apomorphine pump continuation is a separate outcome from motor benefit: a retrospective 110-patient study reported 35% discontinuation over two years and stable quality of life among continuers despite sustained motor-fluctuation reduction; another 208-patient cohort found that many discontinuations were switches to DBS, so discontinuation is not synonymous with drug failure. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-021-00194-7 · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13347506/
- [statement] A 2013 expert review states that very few comparative studies have evaluated the three device-aided therapies for specific motor problems and identifies the type of motor problems, age, and cognitive and psychiatric status as variables relevant to choosing among DBS, apomorphine infusion and duodenal/jejunal levodopa infusion. A 2024 review of advanced therapies states that there is no age limit for LCIG/LECIG and CSAI while an age limit for DBS is often discussed, that dementia is a clear contraindication for CSAI and DBS, that severe orthostatic hypotension and severe psychosis are contraindications for CSAI, and that frequent falls with injuries might be a contraindication for DBS. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3825542/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/
- [statement] Apparent differences between device therapies in observational comparisons require caution: baseline differences can confound outcomes, and retrospective matching cannot remove all selection effects. The 2025 cohort also lacked systematic safety-data collection, preventing a full benefit-risk comparison. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10310730/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01093-x
- [statement] FDA's Drugs@FDA record for NDA 216962 lists the original approval of Vyalev (foscarbidopa and foslevodopa) injection on 10/16/2024; the FDA approval letter states that the NDA provides for subcutaneous use for the treatment of motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson's disease and acknowledges an August 16, 2024 amendment that constituted a complete response to FDA's June 18, 2024 action letter. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/daf/index.cfm?event=overview.process&ApplNo=216962 · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2024/216962Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- [statement] FDA's Drugs@FDA record for NDA 214056 lists the original approval of Onapgo (apomorphine hydrochloride) injection on 02/03/2025; the FDA approval letter states that the NDA provides for the treatment of motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson's disease and acknowledges an August 1, 2024 amendment that constituted a complete response to FDA's April 5, 2024 action letter. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/daf/index.cfm?event=overview.process&ApplNo=214056 · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2025/214056Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- [statement] The European Medicines Agency's Onerji page states that Onerji (levodopa/carbidopa) received a marketing authorisation valid throughout the EU on 27 April 2026, for motor fluctuations in patients with advanced Parkinson's disease that are not sufficiently controlled by oral anti-Parkinson medicinal products; the manufacturer's announcement identifies Onerji as project code ND0612, a continuous subcutaneous infusion of liquid levodopa/carbidopa. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/onerji · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://neuroderm.com/our-company/news-and-events/eu-marketing-authorization-for-onerji/
- [statement] NICE's topic-prioritisation page for levodopa/carbidopa (ND0612) for Parkinson's disease [ID6727] records the decision "Not selected" with a decision publication date of 25 November 2026; the topic had been selected for technology appraisal in December 2025 and was deselected because the product is not a new active substance or a significant licence extension. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-25) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/awaiting-development/gid-ta11954 · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] The 2022 EAN/MDS-ES guideline on invasive therapies states that STN-DBS is the best-studied intervention for advanced Parkinson's disease with fluctuations not satisfactorily controlled with oral medications and that treatment should be offered to eligible patients, that GPi-DBS can also be offered, that DBS should not be offered to people with early Parkinson's disease without fluctuations, and that LCIG and an apomorphine pump can be considered for advanced Parkinson's disease with fluctuations not sufficiently managed with oral treatments. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35791766/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] A 2022 Bayesian network meta-analysis associated LCIG and DBS with greater six-month OFF-time and quality-of-life improvement than apomorphine infusion or best medical therapy, with no significant LCIG-versus-DBS difference. Its indirect comparison mixed randomised and non-randomised studies, and carried three-month LCIG/apomorphine trial outcomes forward to six months. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9712309/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] A 2019 meta-analysis of five cohort studies involving 257 patients found no significant LCIG-versus-STN-DBS difference in UPDRS-III motor scores or adverse events; UPDRS-IV improvement favored STN-DBS, with substantial heterogeneity. Lack of significance does not establish equivalence. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6718716/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] In the 12-week active-controlled phase 3 foslevodopa-foscarbidopa trial, the incremental gain in ON time without troublesome dyskinesia versus oral immediate-release levodopa-carbidopa was 1·75 h; the incremental OFF-time reduction was 1·79 h. This was a comparison with oral therapy, not DBS or intestinal infusion. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36402160/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] In that foslevodopa-foscarbidopa trial, adverse events caused premature discontinuation in 16 of 74 infusion participants (22%) versus one of 67 oral-treatment participants (1%); infusion-site events were common. These trial-specific rates should not be used as a cross-device safety league table. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36402160/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] A 2026 systematic review pooling subcutaneous levodopa and foslevodopa regimens found clinically meaningful OFF-time improvement versus oral levodopa, but patient-experience gains were statistically rather than clinically significant, with more infusion-site adverse events; these findings do not compare the pumps directly with DBS. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12853972/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] The 2024 review associates intestinal levodopa therapies with tube displacement, wound problems or infections, abdominal pain and polyneuropathy. It describes apomorphine infusion-site nodules, nausea, somnolence and possible impulse-control disorders; these are therapy-specific risks rather than a single common device-risk profile. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] A 2025 retrospective cohort compared 295 people continuing oral therapy with 313 transitioning to device-aided therapy, including 284 DBS and 29 enteral levodopa recipients. Mean 12-month PDQ-39 summary-index change was −5.0 in the device group versus +0.9 in the oral group; these are pooled observational outcomes, not a randomized pump-versus-DBS comparison. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01093-x · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] The 2025 study authors interpret their pooled cohort as showing meaningful quality-of-life improvement after device therapy. Zheng and Liu’s 2026 commentary accepts the observed improvement but questions causal interpretation because of residual candidacy confounding, differing baseline definitions and pooling DBS with enteral levodopa. The commentary identifies possible bias rather than proving the benefits are absent. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01093-x · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01342-7

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Delivery route changes invasiveness: subcutaneous apomorphine or levodopa avoids the intestinal tube procedure, intestinal levodopa requires a PEG-J system, and DBS requires intracranial electrode implantation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592668/
- [statement] Intestinal levodopa bypasses gastric emptying to provide more stable plasma levodopa levels than oral dosing; subcutaneous levodopa is another continuous delivery strategy that avoids surgical jejunal tube placement. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12853972/
- [statement] Reviews of device-assisted therapy state that device selection depends on individual patient factors such as age, comorbidities, therapy-specific risks and patient preferences, and a single-centre comparison lists treatment availability, cost of treatment and local expertise as further considerations. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10310730/
- [statement] External pumps require daily preparation and site or tube care, often with caregiver support; DBS exchanges this daily external-pump burden for neurosurgery and continuing device follow-up. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592668/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11875732/
- [statement] A 2023 non-randomised single-centre comparison included 66 patients (13 apomorphine, 19 LCIG, 34 STN-DBS); DBS recipients had better baseline profiles. Quality-of-life and motor outcomes improved with LCIG and DBS, while apomorphine changes were not statistically significant. The baseline imbalance prevents a causal treatment ranking. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10310730/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] OFF-time reduction alone does not guarantee a clinically important quality-of-life gain; this distinction appears in subcutaneous levodopa synthesis and long-term apomorphine experience. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12853972/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-021-00194-7
- [statement] Intestinal levodopa gel bypasses swallowing and gastric passage through a jejunal tube and an external pump; DBS requires implantation of electrodes and a pulse generator. Subcutaneous apomorphine and foslevodopa/foscarbidopa avoid the implantation surgery required for these other approaches. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6995127/
- [statement] The 2024 individualized-treatment review describes foslevodopa/foscarbidopa as a soluble prodrug formulation permitting continuous subcutaneous delivery over a 24-hour period. It reports infusion-site erythema, nodules, cellulitis and pain, as well as visual hallucinations, among adverse effects. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS
- [statement] Daily device work matters in treatment choice: LCIG and apomorphine pumps require cartridge changes and handling, often with relative or nursing support. DBS still requires specialist follow-up and rechargeable systems require charging; discussions should include maintenance, lifestyle and caregiver needs. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502575/ · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3825542/
- [statement] The Michael J. Fox Foundation reported on February 3, 2026 that ND0612, an under-the-skin infusion of levodopa and carbidopa, had received a second FDA Complete Response Letter; it states that the FDA sent a first Complete Response Letter in June 2024 and, after the company's May 2025 resubmission, issued the second in October 2025. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-03) — https://www.michaeljfox.org/news/second-fda-response-letter-issued-nd0612-therapy · keywords: Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS

## Research summary — Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS

Device-aided therapies address disabling motor fluctuations inadequately controlled by oral treatment. Subcutaneous apomorphine and levodopa pumps, intestinal levodopa infusion and DBS differ in invasiveness, daily management and adverse effects. Comparative cohorts and indirect meta-analyses suggest benefits but cannot establish a universal winner because selection and baseline differences matter. Subcutaneous foslevodopa has randomised evidence against oral levodopa, alongside infusion-site reactions and treatment withdrawals. FDA records show Vyalev and Onapgo approved in 2024 and 2025; ND0612 has had two FDA Complete Response Letters and an EU authorisation in 2026.

## Source disagreement — Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS

The 2025 cohort authors emphasize clinically meaningful pooled quality-of-life gains; Zheng and Liu’s 2026 commentary argues that residual confounding, time-zero asymmetry and pooling limit causal interpretation. This is a methodological disagreement, not evidence that either device is ineffective.

## Open question — Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS

How do modern subcutaneous levodopa systems compare directly with DBS and intestinal infusion over matched long-term follow-up?
